title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Ops Playbook
author: Ava Chen
content:
Summary:
This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel-scheduling design, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, recent release notes, known issues, and day-2 runbooks. It is the canonical reference for oncall, performance engineers, and anyone making changes that affect inference latency, throughput, or stability.

Audience:
- Serving runtime engineers
- SRE and capacity planning
- Benchmarks / perf owners
- Private deployment integrators

1) Overview
The Redwood serving runtime is a GPU-optimized inference stack designed for high throughput, low latency, and predictable economics across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. This doc describes:
- logical components,
- kernel scheduling and placement policies,
- profiling and tracing playbook,
- benchmark harness and CI integration,
- release highlights and known issues, and
- operational runbooks for common incidents.

2) Runtime architecture (high level)
Components:
- API Frontend (route handling, auth, rate limits)
- Router / Smart Router (policy routing by latency/cost/region/model)
- Request Broker / Scheduler (assigns requests to workers, handles batching)
- Worker Runtime (model runner on GPU, NVMe-backed KV cache, local batching queues)
- KV Cache Service (shared prefix/cache layer for hot prompts)
- Metrics & Tracing (Prometheus, OpenTelemetry)
- Control Plane (deployment config, rollouts, model catalog)

Data flow (simplified):
1. Frontend authenticates and validates request.
2. Router selects a target pool using policy (latency SLO, cost tier, model compatibility).
3. Scheduler computes batching window and assigns to a Worker.
4. Worker checks KV cache/embedding cache and may short-circuit or hit model.
5. Worker executes optimized kernels, updates KV cache, streams tokens back.

Key design decisions:
- Continuous batching with per-model dynamic target batch sizes to balance p95 latency and throughput.
- Kernel selection at runtime based on model topology, seq-len, and hardware capabilities (FP16, quantized kernels).
- Smart fallback: if a requested model variant is unavailable, route to a compatible quantized/latency-optimized variant with traceable fallback marker.

3) Kernel scheduling and placement
Goals:
- Maximize GPU utilization while protecting latency SLOs.
- Avoid noisy neighbor interference across clients and QoS tiers.

Scheduler primitives and policies:
- Worker queues: separate priority queues per customer tier (interactive vs batch).
- Affinity groups: pin long-running KV-heavy sessions to the same GPU to benefit from warm KV caches and KV cache memory locality.
- Preemption: short interactive requests can preempt lower-priority batch jobs with graceful cancellation and retry policies.
- Kernel selector: picks a sequence of kernels (matmul, attention, rotary, layernorm) tuned for sequence length and quantization.

Example scheduler config (YAML):
---
scheduler:
  max_concurrent_infers_per_gpu: "32"
  priority_queues: ["interactive", "reserved", "batch"]
  preemption:
    enabled: "true"
    grace_period_ms: "120"
  affinity:
    kv_warm_threshold: "1000" # requests per hour to enable session pinning
---

Heuristics used at runtime:
- If p95 latency > target for two consecutive minutes, reduce target batch size by 20% on affected workers.
- If GPU SM utilization < 30% and p95 < SLO, increase batch timeout (up to configured cap).

4) Profiling & tracing playbook
Objectives:
- Reproduce high-latency or low-throughput scenarios locally.
- Identify kernel hotspots and memory stalls.
- Validate kernel selector correctness and quantization impact.

Tools and signals:
- perf / eBPF: syscall and kernel-level blocking (useful for PCIe/backplane stalls).
- Nsight Systems / Nsight Compute: kernel-level GPU hotspot analysis.
- nvprof (legacy) for quick GPU traces.
- pprof (Go) and flamegraphs for scheduler/front-end hotspots.
- OTEL traces and distributed traces (trace-id) for end-to-end latency.
- runtime-profiler (internal) \u2014 collects combined CPU/GPU traces in our format.

Standard profiling procedure:
1. Collect a golden workload (bench/testset) that reproduces the issue.
2. Run OTEL trace with sampling=100% for the problematic route:
   curl -H "X-Trace: 1" -X POST https://api.redwood.local/generate -d @request.json 
3. Snapshot Prometheus metrics for the window (token-rate, latency_histograms, gpu_utilization, memory_alloc).
4. Run Nsight Systems on a single affected worker:
   sudo nsys profile --output=nsys-report ./bin/worker --config=...
5. Collect pprof from scheduler process:
   go tool pprof -http=:8080 http://scheduler:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30
6. Correlate timeline: scheduler latency -> queue time -> kernel time. Flag any >50% queue time as scheduling edge case.

Required metrics to collect (minimum):
- request.queue_time_ms
- infer.kernel_time_ms (per-layer breakdown if available)
- gpu.sm_utilization_pct
- gpu.memory_alloc_pct
- p50/p95/p99 latency (end-to-end + worker-only)
- batch_size_distribution

Tracing artifacts & retention:
- Store combined traces in S3 under s3://redwood-traces/serving/<YYYY-MM-DD>/trace-<id>.json
- Keep profiler artifacts for 90 days. After that, summary artifacts are retained 1 year.

5) Benchmarking suite and CI integration
Scope:
- Microbenchmarks: kernel latencies (matmul, attention) across sequence lengths and batch sizes.
- Macrobenchmarks: end-to-end request latency and token-per-second for commonly used models (Llama-2-13B, MPT-7B, OPT-30B, and Redwood-curated variants).
- Stress tests: long-running traffic with tail-latency monitoring and KV hit/miss patterns.

Harness characteristics:
- Parameterized by model, batch_size, seq_len, concurrent_clients, and token_length.
- Deterministic request templates and RNG seeds for reproducibility.
- Outputs JSON reports with per-model: p50/p95/p99, tokens/s, avg_batch_size, kernel_breakdown (ms).

How to run (example):
   ./bench/run-benchmark --model llm-13b-q8 --concurrency 64 --seq-len 512 --duration 300 --out report-13b.json

CI integration:
- Nightly CI runs full micro + macro suite for each supported instance type (A100-80GB, H100-80GB, L4-48GB).
- Regression alerts: if p95 or tokens/s deviates >7% from baseline, notify #perf-regressions and open a Jira.
- Benchmarks are versioned and stored at s3://redwood-benchmarks/<commit-hash>/report.json

Result format (JSON fields):
- model, instance_type, date, commit_hash, p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, tokens_per_sec, avg_batch_size, notes

6) Release notes (selected / recent)
- 2027-02-28: Kernel selector v2 deployed \u2014 improved matmul tiling for seq_len > 1024, reduced p95 by 18% on long-seq workloads.
- 2027-01-10: Adaptive preemption introduced to reduce batch interference for interactive requests.
- 2026-12-15: Default quantized kernel (q8) added for MPT family; requires model flag enable_q8=true.

7) Known issues (operational)
1. Intermittent GPU page faults on H100 when concurrent memcpy + kernels spike.
   - Symptom: worker OOM or long stalls, nv-hostengine messages in dmesg.
   - Workaround: drain and restart worker, set CUDA_ASYNC_COPY=0 for affected workers until patch applied.
2. p99 tail latency spikes when KV cache miss rate > 40% for multi-turn chat.
   - Mitigation: pin sessions (affinity) for high-turn customers and increase KV cache memory for selected pools.
3. Scheduler deadlock under extreme churn of small sessions (sub-50-token requests).
   - Detection: queue_time_ms steadily increases while kernel_time stays low.
   - Workaround: increase small-request fast-path threads and enable per-customer rate-limits.
4. Quantized kernel numerical regressions for rare ops in model X (reported in model onboarding).
   - Action: mark model as restricted_quantized and fallback to fp16 until patch; owners alerted.

8) Runtime runbooks (play-by-play)
A) High p95 latency for interactive endpoints
1. Check Grafana: route-level p95 and worker p95.
2. Check queue_time_ms vs kernel_time_ms to localize (scheduling vs kernel).
3. If queue_time_ms dominant: inspect scheduler pprof and recent config changes; consider scaling workers or reducing batch window.
4. If kernel_time_ms dominant: pull latest Nsight trace for hotspot and check kernel selector logs (metrics: kernel_choice, fallback).
5. Short-term mitigation: enable dedicated pool (priority=interactive) and set max_batch_timeout_ms=30.
6. Escalation: ping serving-runtime oncall (PagerDuty) and assign to perf owner.

B) GPU OOM on worker
1. Identify the container / pod and kill gracefully: kubectl delete pod <pod> --grace-period=30
2. Check worker logs for "cudaMalloc failed" and model memory estimates.
3. Increase worker memory cap or reduce reserved_cache_size and redeploy.
4. If happening across many nodes, mark instance series in autoscaler to remove from pool and notify eng-infra.

C) Repro for model regression (quality or perf)
1. Pin to previous model version via control plane and capture golden eval set.
2. Run bench harness and profiling steps to compare kernel timings and output diffs.
3. If numerical regression suspected, open model-onboarding ticket and add to regression triage board.

Appendix A \u2014 Quick commands
- Grab scheduler pprof: curl http://scheduler:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30 -o scheduler-pprof.pb
- Run Nsight Systems: sudo nsys profile --output=/tmp/nsys-worker ./bin/worker --instance-id=worker-123
- Run benchmark: ./bench/run-benchmark --model llm-13b-q8 --concurrency 64 --duration 300 --out report-13b.json

Appendix B \u2014 SLOs and thresholds (operational)
- Interactive p95 (end-to-end): "200ms"
- Interactive p99 (end-to-end): "450ms"
- Worker kernel p95: "150ms"
- Error rate (5xx) SLA: "<0.1%"
- Target GPU SM utilization for cost-efficiency: "50\u201385%"
